awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: Bayesian Inversion Approaches to Partial Differential Equations: Theory, Algorithm Development, and Applications
awd_abstract_narration:
The project will contribute to a new and rapidly developing area of applied mathematics rich with applications for modeling and challenges for rigorous mathematical analysis. This research will yield important new methods for modeling chemical mixing, biologically active fluids, and geophysical systems. Improving methods for these domain settings will provide more effective tools to address important problems such as the spread of pathogens or pollutants or to quantify the degree and type of climate hazards. The investigators will develop new methodologies for calibrating and designing effective measurement strategies of these various fluid systems, which simultaneously resolve degrees of the inherent uncertainty in these measurements. This project involves the training and active participation of a number of graduate students and other earlier career scientists. The cross institutional and cross disciplinary nature of this project will provide unique opportunities for the participants.
 
Recent advances in computational infrastructure combined with novel mathematical formulations and newly discovered algorithms have allowed the extension of the Bayesian approach to new classes of physics-constrained inverse problems. Solutions typically take many times the computational power of a single solve of a nonlinear forward map based on a partial differential equations (PDEs) where the estimation concerns a function rather than a finite collection of numerical values, namely where we are interested in estimating an infinite-dimensional unknown parameter. The investigators will undertake a research program at the intersection of stochastic and functional analysis, high-performance computing, nonlinear PDEs, and fluid dynamics. Specifically, the investigators will (1) consider a series of physically motivated PDE inverse problems with infinite-dimensional unknowns; (2) develop novel algorithms adapted to efficiently sample from infinite-dimensional measures; (3) develop the ergodic theory for certain classes of infinite-dimensional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms to rigorously assess rates of convergence in sampling target posterior measures; and (4) analyze consistency in the large data observation limit for infinite dimensional models. The project contributes effective frameworks for the measurement of turbulent fluid flows from sparse, irregular data while developing sampling methods of broader interest across computational statistics and data science.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project advanced the mathematical and computational foundations of Bayesian inference for physical models governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). This is an exciting frontier of statistical inference that provides a principled approach to estimating phenomena ranging from fluid flows and heat conduction to biological transport, seismic hazards, and even quantum physics. In many scientific settings, the quantities of greatest interest—the turbulent velocity field driving an ocean current, the disordered potential governing electron transport in a nanowire, the subsurface geology shaping seismic risk—cannot be observed directly but must instead be inferred from indirect, incomplete, and noisy measurements. Our research developed new mathematical theory, computational algorithms, and real-world applications to address these challenges within a rigorous statistical framework.

Intellectual Merit

A major thrust of this project was the development of novel Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling algorithms—the computational engine underlying modern Bayesian inference with broad applications across the sciences. Our starting point is the preconditioned Crank–Nicolson (pCN) algorithm, a foundational method whose effectiveness does not degrade as the number of unknowns grows—a critical property for the infinite-dimensional problems arising in PDE-based inference. We developed several new methods that extend and enrich this idea in complementary directions: multiproposal pCN (mpCN), which exploits parallel computing architectures by evaluating clouds of proposals simultaneously; surrogate-gradient preconditioned Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, which incorporates derivative information without requiring the numerically expensive exact gradients of the forward model; and multiproposal Elliptical Slice Sampling, which achieves similar dimension-free performance while automatically tuning its own step size. Each of these methods addresses the same broad class of PDE inverse problems but offers distinct computational trade-offs suited to different settings. Two theoretical perspectives proved essential for understanding and advancing these algorithms. First, we developed a comprehensive "involutive" mathematical framework for classifying bias-free Metropolis-type algorithms that revealed deep structural connections between these methods—connections not apparent from their original formulations—and guided the discovery of several new ones. Second, the study of the large proposal limit, in which the number of proposals in multiproposal methods grows without bound, exposed further relationships between algorithm classes and provided a powerful lens for analyzing their behavior. Together with the weak Harris theorem, these tools enabled a rigorous study of mixing rates that places the practical effectiveness of these methods on firm theoretical footing. Taken together, these advances bring the practical resolution of large-scale PDE inverse problems squarely into view. Related work extended these ideas to improve phylogenetic inference in computational biology, yielding significant speedups in estimating evolutionary histories from genomic data.

In parallel, we made foundational contributions to the long-time behavior and numerical accuracy of stochastic PDEs from fluid dynamics, including the stochastic Navier–Stokes and Korteweg–de Vries equations, as well as models of heat conduction and electroconvection. These results ensure that computational simulations remain faithful to the true dynamics over long time horizons and develop analytical techniques—particularly around ergodicity and stability of invariant measures—that share deep connections with the convergence theory underpinning our MCMC methods.

We also advanced the theoretical foundations of Bayesian consistency for PDE inverse problems—establishing that, as more data is collected, statistical estimates provably concentrate on the true unknown. This ongoing work develops an abstract framework applicable to a broad class of problems, drawing on tools from functional analysis, probability theory, and optimal transport, and clarifying fundamental barriers to consistency specific to PDE-informed statistical models.

The project produced 10 published journal articles in leading venues (including the Transactions of the AMS, Annals of Applied Probability, and Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences), 1 book chapter in the second edition of the influential Handbook of Markov Chain Monte Carlo, 1 article in press, 2 submitted manuscripts, and a number of additional works in advanced stages of preparation.

Broader Impacts

The methods developed in this project were applied to problems of direct societal relevance. In geophysics, we developed a Bayesian framework for estimating earthquake magnitudes from sparse historical records, addressing the challenge of hazard assessment in data-limited settings. In quantum computing, we developed new statistical diagnostics for detecting undesirable disorder in superconducting nanowire devices being developed for topological quantum computation. In computational biology, our algorithms contributed to improved inference of viral evolutionary dynamics, with applications to Dengue, Hepatitis C, and Lassa virus.

The project provided extensive training and mentorship opportunities. One PhD student completed his dissertation under this award, and five additional PhD students at various institutions were mentored through collaborative research projects. Two postdoctoral researchers received sustained mentorship and professional development. Research findings were disseminated broadly through 21 invited talks at universities and international conferences, the organization of a major workshop and six conference sessions, and leadership of three seminar series. The PI also developed and taught graduate courses on Monte Carlo sampling methods, with an ongoing textbook project that will make these advanced techniques accessible to a wider audience of students and researchers.
